article.title: These Stunning Fractals Are Made of Snow
article.summary: Simon Beck treats big stretches of untouched snow as a blank canvas. He plans each design on paper, then walks it out in snowshoes, using a compass and counted paces to keep the geometry accurate. His favorite subjects are fractals, which are patterns that repeat at smaller and smaller scales, such as Koch snowflakes and Sierpinski triangles. The piece shows how a cold, empty landscape can hold very precise mathematics.
facts: Beck makes his designs on foot, so every line is a trail of snowshoe prints.
He gets from sketch to snow using only a compass and pace counting, drawing on a background in engineering and orienteering.
One of his designs is a snow version of the Sierpinski triangle, a fractal described in 1915. Similar patterns show up in artwork centuries older.
Beck has said he started adding fractals after reading James Gleick's book about chaos theory.
questions: Why might a vast, empty snowfield be a better place for mathematical art than a gallery wall?
If an artwork will vanish with the next snowfall, what is the value of making it precisely?
Where else in nature do you see patterns that repeat at smaller scales, and could you recreate one with just your feet and a compass?

related.t: Association of Polar Early Career Scientists - Polar Art

alt.title: Crafty Geometry
alt.summary: Mathematicians are using knitting and crochet to make physical models of surfaces that are very hard to picture. Crocheted versions of the hyperbolic plane, a counterintuitive curved shape, let students and researchers handle and explore its odd properties. The article also looks at wider craft math, including patterns for Möbius scarves and Klein bottle hats. Yarn turns out to be a good way to see ideas that mathematicians already know.
facts: In 1901, David Hilbert proved that a smooth model of the hyperbolic plane can't be built, because the surface buckles.
One mathematician looked at a crocheted hyperbolic plane and exclaimed that this is what they really look like.
A mathematician at Mercer University says knitting and crocheting help her see familiar math in a different light.
The article suggests swapping the holiday sweater for a Möbius scarf, a Klein bottle hat or hyperbolic ornaments.
questions: Why might a handmade model teach something that equations and drawings can't?
What other crafts you know of, such as weaving, quilting or origami, might hide serious mathematics?
If a shape can't be built smoothly, what does it mean to say it exists?

article.title: Coral in crisis: Stories from the front line
article.summary: This feature visits four communities whose livelihoods depend on reefs that are getting more fragile. It opens in Shenzhen, China, where one conservationist has spent about two decades building underwater coral nurseries to stitch broken corals back together. It then moves to Bali, which sits inside the Coral Triangle, and on to Africa and the Americas. The stories show how warming seas and local pressures reach ordinary people who depend on reefs for tourism and food.
facts: Coral covered about 70% of Shenzhen's Dapeng Bay in the 1980s, before decades of damage.
A 30-hectare protected zone there was set up after the 1996 El Niño to rebuild fish stocks and heal the reef.
The Coral Triangle spans six nations and holds about 76% of the world's coral species.
Bali's reefs draw divers hoping to see mola mola (ocean sunfish) and manta rays.
questions: If a coral nursery can take two decades to make a difference, how should we judge whether restoration is working?
How do tourism income and reef protection help or harm each other in places like Bali?
What can communities far from the ocean do about a problem that is driven by global heat?

alt.title: Two decades of research show Indonesia's coral reefs are heat-tolerant — but only up to a point
alt.summary: Researchers pooled long-term coral monitoring records from across Indonesia, home to the world's largest and most biodiverse reef system. They found that live coral cover held steady under low to moderate heat stress. It then fell sharply once accumulated heat passed a clear threshold. The authors argue that Indonesia needs a more coordinated national system to track reef condition and bleaching.
facts: Indonesia's reefs cover more than 32,000 square kilometres across the archipelago.
Coral cover dropped sharply once heat stress passed about 12 degree-heating weeks.
Degree-heating weeks work like a running 'heat dose', combining how much warmer the water is than usual and how long it stays that way.
Stable total coral cover can hide losses, such as fewer branching or old corals and less complex reef structure.
questions: Why might a reef look healthy by one measure while quietly losing its structure and diversity?
What would a good national coral-monitoring system look like in a country with thousands of islands?
If there's a heat threshold beyond which reefs collapse, how should that change conservation priorities?

related.t: An Exciting Discovery for Tropical Pacific Corals (NOAA/AOML)

article.title: De-Ratting Rat Island Brought Silent Ecosystem Back to Life
article.summary: Rats escaped from a shipwreck in the 1780s onto a remote Aleutian island and wiped out its seabird colonies. The island was eventually cleared of rats using bait dropped by conservation teams. Roughly a decade later, researchers found the seabirds back and the whole shoreline ecosystem recovering. The shore now looks like nearby islands that rats never reached. It shows that some damaged ecosystems can bounce back surprisingly fast.
facts: The rats arrived by accident. They were stowaways on a shipwreck in the 1780s.
The rats' effects reached far past the birds. They disrupted the food chain all the way down to algae.
Surveys five and 11 years after the rats were removed showed steady recovery. The shoreline now has more kelp and fewer marine invertebrates.
The island was renamed Hawadax, which restores its original Aleut name.
questions: Why can a single accidental arrival, like stowaway rats, change an entire island ecosystem so completely?
Rat removal helped the kelp as well as the birds. What does that say about how connected land and sea ecosystems are?
If an island can recover in about a decade, how should we decide which invasive-species problems are worth the cost and risk of eradication?

related.t: 'Island of Rats' Recovers - UC San Diego Today
New Seabird Life at Hawadax Island Alaska - The Nature Conservancy

alt.title: How a tiny wasp could save Christmas Island's spectacular red crabs from crazy ants
alt.summary: On Christmas Island, invasive yellow crazy ants are a major threat to the famous red crabs. The ants' giant colonies depend on honeydew from another invasive species, the yellow lac scale insect. Parks Australia planned to release a tiny wasp that attacks the scale insects, which would cut off the ants' food supply. Researchers also tested whether the wasps would still attack scale insects that ants were tending, and they did.
facts: The wasp is only about 2 millimetres long.
Crazy ant supercolonies need a steady food source. Another invasive species, the scale insect, supplies it.
Parks Australia had already tried many methods against the ants, including aerial and hand baiting.
Tests showed the wasps still attack scale insects that ants are guarding.
questions: What are the risks of fighting one invasive species by releasing another organism, and how could scientists reduce them?
Why do the red crabs matter so much to the island's forests?
How might several invasive species end up helping each other, and what does that mean for how we manage them?

related.t: Christmas Island Yellow Crazy Ant Control Program (Australian Government)

article.title: Researchers Are Using Artificial Intelligence to Reconstruct Ancient Games
article.summary: A team of software engineers, game historians and archaeologists at Maastricht University is trying to work out how long-lost ancient board games were really played. Their Digital Ludeme Project breaks each game into basic building blocks, a bit like genes. AI then plays thousands of candidate rule sets against itself to find the ones that actually work. The goal is to trace how games changed across time and places, like a game of telephone.
facts: Tutankhamun's tomb held four senet sets, an Egyptian game tied to the journey to the afterlife.
The project calls the basic building blocks of games 'ludemes', which are essentially game genes.
Once games are mapped this way, researchers can count the steps needed for one game to evolve into another, called 'ludemic distance'.
Testing rules means playing the game many, many times to find spots where it breaks down, becomes unfair, or can't be won.
questions: If nobody wrote down the rules of a game, how confident can we ever be that a reconstruction matches what ancient players did?
What might the way games spread and mutate tell us about how ideas and cultures moved around the ancient world?
Is a rule set that an AI finds balanced and fun necessarily the same one that people played thousands of years ago?

related.t: Senet and Twenty Squares: Two Board Games Played by Ancient Egyptians
AI for Ancient Games (Report on the Digital Ludeme Project)

alt.title: Mystery stone is actually ancient Roman board game
alt.summary: A carved stone from a Roman-era site in the Dutch city of Heerlen puzzled archaeologists for decades because nobody knew whether it was a game board or something else. Researchers worked with AI programmers at Maastricht University to build a system that learned from the rules of about 100 ancient games from the region. The system, called Ludii, produced many possible rule sets, played them against itself, and picked out variants that people would enjoy. The team named the game Ludus Coriovalli.
facts: The AI program's name, Ludii, is a play on the Latin word for games.
Two AI agents played 1,000 games for each rule set, and the team tested 130 combinations of starting, movement and ending rules.
The results suggest a blocking game, which pushes the earliest evidence for that type of game in Europe back by several centuries, from the medieval period to Roman times.
The researchers compared the wear patterns the AI games produced with the real scuffs on the stone to judge which rules fit.
questions: What counts as good evidence that an object was a game rather than, say, an architectural sketch?
How could AI-simulated play help archaeologists with other mystery objects?
If the AI picks rules that humans find fun, are we discovering the past or inventing a new game?

related.t: Researchers crack the rules of unknown board game from the Roman period (Leiden University)
AI simulation helps calculate the rules of an unknown Roman board game (Antiquity)
